newsitem.title: USA: US corporate bonds flat but for Conrail.
newsitem.headline: US corporate bonds flat but for Conrail.

text.p: U.S. corporate bonds put in a quiet session on Tuesday and ended mostly unchanged, while high-yielders followed suit, dealers said.
Conrail Inc debt proved to be one deviation from the norm as the 9-3/4s of 2020 widened about eight points following the announcement of an $8.4 billion merger with CSX Corp, according to traders.
Only a handful of desks reported seeing any bonds trade around the news, however.

The merger would create a freight transportation company with over $14 billion in annual revenues. Under the terms of the pact, about 19.9 percent of Conrail's outstanding voting shares will be acquired by CSX for about $92.50 per share. The remaining shares will be acquired for stock at an exchange ratio of 1.85619 CSX shares for each Conrail share.

Standard & Poor's and Moody's Investors Service said they may lower their respective BBB-minus and A3 senior debt ratings of CSX Corp. S&P also said it may cut Conrail's single-A corporate credit rating.

In other ratings news, S&P affirmed Rite Aid Corp's BBB-plus senior unsecured debt and said it may raise the B-plus corporate rating of Thrify Payless. The action follows the proposed $2.3 billion merger of the companies, which includes Rite Aid's assumption of $890 million in debt.

The Conrail/CSX news was the only bump in an otherwise quiet trading session as the street returned from a long weekend and prepared for another swath of issuance. Last week featured about $6.0 billion of straight corporate debt.
Prices held at previous closing levels as U.S. Treasuries marked time ahead of October consumer price data on Wednesday.

Only one new issue priced on Tuesday. Citicorp issued $200 million subordinated notes due 2011 as 7-1/4s to yield 7.335 percent or 77 basis points over the Treasury curve. The notes are rated A2 by Moody's and single-A by S&P.
Looking ahead, deals expected to come to market include $100 million in debt from Goodyear via Morgan Stanley and $300 million from British Sky Broadcasting, sources said.

Turning to the corporate high-yield sector prices were mostly unchanged; however, Harrah's Jazz bonds were seen trading up a point, traders said. The debt closed at 57-1/2 to 58-1/2 with no sellers, one trader said.
Street talk that suggested Harrah's jazz and the bondholders committee are close to a pact regarding the treatment of bondholders claims under a reorganization plan spurred the move, traders said.
"If it was a fact there was an agreement the bonds would have shot up even more," one high-yield trader said. "Just the rumor drove the bonds up a point."
In the governments market, the benchmark 30-year bond closed up 1/32 to 98-26/32 to yield 6.84 percent.
